subject: Accounting
title: Adjusting for Prepaid Expenses
description: One-minute skill: Adjusting for Prepaid Expenses.

hook.text: You pay $12,000 for a full year of insurance in January. Is the entire amount a January expense?

buildup.text: Prepaid expenses are costs paid in advance for future benefit—insurance, rent, subscriptions.

discovery.text: Each month, $1,000 moves from prepaid insurance (asset) to insurance expense—matching the period.

twist.text: Without this adjustment, January looks expensive and the next 11 months look free—distorting profits.

climax.text: Adjusting entries ensure each period bears only the costs it actually consumed.

punchline.text: Pay once, expense monthly. Matching demands it.

quiz.question: How are prepaid expenses adjusted?
options: By moving the used portion from asset to expense each period
By recording the full amount immediately
By ignoring them until year end

details.summary: Prepaid expenses are payments made in advance for future benefits—like insurance or rent. This topic explains how to record the initial payment as an asset and then systematically expense it over the periods that benefit from it.
details.whyItMatters: Mishandling prepaid expenses distorts both the balance sheet and income statement. Proper adjustment ensures each period bears only its fair share of the cost.
takeaways: Prepaid expenses start as assets on the balance sheet, not as expenses
Adjusting entries gradually move the cost from asset to expense as time passes
Common prepaids include insurance premiums, rent deposits, and annual subscriptions

faq.question: What is a prepaid expense in bookkeeping?
faq.answer: A prepaid expense is a payment made for goods or services that will be consumed in the future. It is initially recorded as an asset and then gradually expensed over the periods that benefit—such as paying 12 months of insurance upfront.

faq.question: How do you adjust prepaid expenses at month-end?
faq.answer: At each month-end, you create an adjusting journal entry that debits the relevant expense account and credits the prepaid asset account for the portion consumed that month. This moves the cost from the balance sheet to the income statement.
